newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic coalition set for poll win, diplomats say.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic coalition set for poll win, diplomats say.

text.p: Slobodan Milosevic's ruling coalition appears set to win Sunday's federal polls, paving the way for the Serbian president to consolidate power and his new rapport with the West, diplomats said on Wednesday.
An opinion poll conducted by the Institute of Economic Sciences of Belgrade University showed this week that 31 percent of those questioned thought Milosevic was Serbia's most trustworthy politician.
The left coalition comprising Milosevic's Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), Yugoslav Left (JUL) and New Democracy (ND) had the support of 45 percent of those surveyed.

Diplomats said Milosevic, once vilified in the West for stoking the fires of sectarian violence in the region, seemed determined to stick to the peacemaking process launched by the U.S.-brokered Dayton accords that ended the war in Bosnia.
They said he had been steadily purging government of nationalist hardliners no longer useful to him and they cited his making peace with old foe Croatia as well as Bosnia's mainly-Moslem government.
His drive for peace was more palatable to the voters than the uncertainty offered by the opposition, despite worsening economic conditions and a wave of strikes, one diplomat said.
"The society is generally conservative, afraid of changes and of the devil they do not know," he said.

In the survey, Milosevic was followed by Dragoslav Avramovic, former National Bank governor, with the support of 27.7 percent of the electorate. He will not be running in Sunday's federal and local elections, however.

For most opposition leaders the poll, surveying 1,520 people, was a disappointment. Results were in single figures, from Vojislav Kostunica, the leader of the Serbian Democratic Party (DSS) at 3.5 percent to Vojislav Seselj of the Radical party with 3.4 percent of popular support.
Zajedno (Together), for example, made up of a broad spectrum of parties ranging from liberals to right-wing nationalists -- could count on only 30 percent of the votes, the poll found.
Diplomats said the lack of Zajedno's coherent policy had hurt its standing and boosted Milosevic's position in the West.
"The only thing these five parties have in common is their desire to topple Milosevic," a Western diplomat told Reuters.
"On all other key issues like the Dayton peace process, relations with other former Yugoslav republic, ethnic and human rights -- they disagree among themselves," he said.
Sunday's vote is seen as a trial run for crucial elections in the Serbian republic next year.
Milosevic's term as Serbian president expires towards the end of 1997 and diplomats believe he will go for the post of president of Yugoslavia.

Victory at the federal level would enable his coalition to amend the constitution and transform the post of federal president to copy the French Constitution which grants the head of state sweeping powers -- and a seven-year mandate.
They said he needed those powers to block veto by nationalists when he tackles the burning issue of human rights in Serbia's mostly-Albanian province of Kosovo.
Belgrade media have reported negotiations on the status of Kosovo scheduled for mid-December in New York.

Political analysts said the best the Kosovo Albanians could hope for were powers of autonomy similar to the territory's status up to 1989 when their autonomy was rescinded on charges that they were moving towards outright seccession.

Once that was settled, Milosevic could expect the outer wall of sanctions against Belgrade to be lifted, giving him access to fresh foreign capital which in turn will alleviate the economic situation in the country, the diplomats said.
